title: Container Geometry, Root Restriction, and Transplanting
objective: Explain how container volume, height, shape, and root occupancy affect water distribution, architecture, and transplant decisions.

terms.definition: Physical limitation of root-system expansion by container boundaries or compacted zones.
Informal term for a root system densely occupying and circling within a container.
Connected water pathway between the transplant root ball and surrounding medium.
Temporary functional decline after transplant caused by root, water, temperature, or handling stress.

coreScience: Container volume limits the space available for roots, water, air, and buffering. Shape matters as well: height changes drainage and average water retention; width changes horizontal exploration; taper and wall design affect circling and root extraction. Nominal volume alone does not describe the root environment.

Restriction can reduce root growth, alter root-to-shoot signaling, and make water and nutrient supply more dependent on frequent management. Dense roots can channel water around the plug or create sharply different moisture zones. Larger containers reduce some constraints but increase wet volume and may remain saturated when occupied by a small plant.

Successful transplanting requires physical contact and moisture continuity between the old root ball and new medium. Large differences in texture, wettability, EC, or moisture can trap roots in the original plug or create drought/saturation interfaces.

cultivationRelevance: Transplant when the plug holds together and roots are actively exploring, before severe circling or repeated daily stress. Readiness is a combined root, shoot, irrigation, and schedule decision.
Match the step-up size to plant demand and the grower's ability to wet the new volume uniformly without keeping it chronically saturated.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Actual volume, height, diameter, drainage, color/material, and prior use.
Coverage by sector, circling, matting, root color, and plug cohesion.
Plant age, shoot size, root-zone moisture, pH/EC, and last irrigation.
Date, new medium/lot, hole preparation, depth, root disturbance, and irrigation.
Wilt, water use, new growth, rooting into new media, and losses.

misconceptions: Bigger containers are always safer: An oversized wet volume can be poorly aerated around a small root system.
Roots instantly use all new media: Colonization takes time and follows suitable water, oxygen, and temperature.
Transplant shock is unavoidable: Good timing, continuity, and handling can greatly reduce it.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis-specific controlled studies isolating container shape and restriction are limited. Much operational guidance comes from general container horticulture and must be validated by cultivar and system.
